column4: Selects inside the delimiters of an object, after an operator or in Visual mode: iw a word, i" a quoted string, i( what is in the parentheses, i{ what is in the braces (diw, ci", yi(, vi[).
Selects an object with its delimiters (and the blanks after a word), after an operator or in Visual mode: aw, a", a(, a{ (daw, ya", va().
Moves the cursor one character left; with a count, that many. It stops at the start of the line.
Moves the cursor one character right; with a count, that many. It stops at the end of the line.
Moves the cursor one line down, keeping the wanted column over shorter lines. After an operator it takes whole lines (dj deletes two lines).
Moves the cursor one line up, keeping the wanted column over shorter lines. After an operator it takes whole lines.
Moves to the start of the next word: a run of letters, digits and underscores, or a run of other symbols that are not blanks. A script change in Japanese text ends a word too.
Moves to the start of the next WORD: anything between blanks.
Moves to the start of this word, or of the one before it when the cursor is already there.
Like b, with WORDs: anything between blanks.
Moves to the last character of this word, or of the next one when the cursor is already there. After an operator the character is included.
Like e, with WORDs: anything between blanks.
Moves to the first column of the line.
Moves to the first character of the line that is not a blank.
Moves to the last character of the line; with a count, of the line that many lines down. After an operator the character is included.
Moves to the last line, or with a count to that line (5G is line 5). The cursor lands on the first non-blank. After an operator it takes whole lines.
Moves to the first line, or with a count to that line (5gg is line 5). After an operator it takes whole lines.
Moves to the next occurrence of the character you type in this line; with a count, the nth one. After an operator the character is included. ; and , repeat it.
Like f, looking back along the line.
Like f, but stops one character before the one found.
Like F, but stops one character after the one found.
Repeats the last f, F, t or T in the same direction.
Repeats the last f, F, t or T in the opposite direction.
Moves from a bracket ( ) [ ] { } at or after the cursor on this line to its partner, skipping nested pairs.
Moves to the next match of the last search, wrapping round the end of the file, and lights the matches. The status line says which one it is, [3/12].
Moves to the previous match of the last search, wrapping round the start of the file.
Searches for the word under the cursor, as a whole word, and moves to its next occurrence.
Searches for the word under the cursor, as a whole word, and moves to its previous occurrence.
Scrolls half a screen down and moves the cursor with it; the line is centered where it can be.
Scrolls half a screen up and moves the cursor with it.
Moves a screen down.
Moves a screen up.
A number before a command repeats it that many times: 3dd, 5j, 2w, 10x. A 0 typed after a number is part of it; alone, 0 is the start of the line.
The word under the cursor, without the blanks around it (iw), or the WORD (iW): diw deletes it, ciw changes it, yiw yanks it, viw selects it.
The word under the cursor with the blanks after it, or before it when there are none (aw), or the WORD (aW).
The text between the pair of quotes on this line that holds the cursor, without the quotes: ci" changes it.
The same with the quotes, and the blanks after the closing one.
The text between the parentheses that hold the cursor, nested pairs counted, without them: ci( changes it. A ( or a ) after i or a means the same.
The same with the parentheses.
The text between the square brackets that hold the cursor, without them.
The same with the square brackets.
The text between the braces that hold the cursor, without them. When the opening brace ends its line and the closing one starts its own, the lines between them as lines.
The same with the braces.
The text between < and > that hold the cursor, without them.
The same with the angle brackets.

d{motion} deletes the text from the cursor to where the motion goes (dw, d$, dip, di"); dd deletes lines; in Visual mode d deletes the selection. What it deletes is what p pastes, and it never goes to the system clipboard ("+d cuts to it); a register name before it ("add) keeps the text there.
c{motion} deletes like d and starts Insert mode; cc changes whole lines; cw changes to the end of the word, as ce does; in Visual mode c changes the selection.

y{motion} copies the text to the unnamed register and to the system clipboard (also through tmux), and says what it took (3 lines yanked); yy yanks lines; in Visual mode y yanks the selection. The text lights up for a moment. With a register name ("ayw) the text stays in sim, even over ssh and tmux: it does not reach the clipboard.

<{motion} takes one level of indent off the lines the motion covers; << is the current line; in Visual mode < outdents the selection. A level is the file's own: 4 columns, 2, or a tab, as the first indented lines show.
>{motion} puts one level of indent on the lines the motion covers; >> is the current line; in Visual mode > indents the selection.

!{motion} opens the command line with the range of lines, ready for a command: !! is the current line, and :{range}!cmd runs the lines through cmd and replaces them with what it prints, as one undo step. Ctrl-c cancels a filter that runs. Not in plain mode.
Deletes the current line, or that many lines with a count (3dd).
Deletes the current line's text, keeping its indent, and starts Insert mode.
Yanks the current line, or that many lines with a count (3yy).
Takes one level of indent off the current line.
Puts one level of indent on the current line.
Opens the command line with the current line as the range, ready for :{range}!cmd.
Deletes from the cursor to the end of the line, as d$.
Deletes from the cursor to the end of the line and starts Insert mode, as c$.
Yanks from the cursor to the end of the line, as y$. In vi Y yanks the whole line (yy does that here).
Deletes the character under the cursor; with a count, that many. In Visual mode x deletes the selection.
Starts Insert mode before the cursor. Esc leaves it.
Starts Insert mode after the cursor.
Starts Insert mode before the first non-blank of the line.
Starts Insert mode at the end of the line.
Opens a new line under this one, with the same indent, and starts Insert mode.
Opens a new line above this one, with the same indent, and starts Insert mode.
Puts the unnamed register (what was last deleted or yanked), or the one named before it ("ap), after the cursor, or under the current line when it holds whole lines; with a count, that many times.
Like p, before the cursor or above the line.
Joins the next line to this one with a single blank; with a count, that many lines.
Replaces the character under the cursor with the one you type; with a count, that many characters.
Undoes the last change, one step at a time. A change that came from the disk and was merged in is a step too.
Redoes what u undid. In vi U undoes a whole line; here it is the key beside u and does what Ctrl-r does.
Redoes what u undid.
Repeats the last change: its keys, with a new count if you give one (3.). Undo is not a change, so . keeps repeating the last real one.

Starts Visual mode on the character, or leaves it. Motions extend the selection, an operator works on it, o jumps to its other end, and i and a with an object select it. The selection is underlined, or gray where the terminal has truecolor.
Starts Visual mode on whole lines, or leaves it.
Moves the cursor to the other end of the selection.
Leaves Insert mode, Visual mode or a half-typed command. In Normal mode with nothing typed it puts the search highlight out (as :noh does).
Cancels a half-typed command or Visual mode; with a filter running it cancels the filter; with nothing to cancel it says q to quit.

column1: {char}	nv	register (a-z A-Z 0-9 - _ + *)	Names the register for the next yank, delete, change or put: ayw yanks into a, "ap puts it. a-z keep their text and A-Z add to it; "0 is the last yank, "1-"9 the last deletes of a line or more ("1p then . puts "2p), "- the small deletes, "_ drops the text, "" is the unnamed one. "+ and "* write the system clipboard (also through tmux) and cannot be read: paste with the terminal. They live in memory only, shared by the open files.

column4: Sets the mark a-z at the cursor's place, in this file: ma, and later 'a comes back to its line and `a to its place, with an operator too (d'a, y`a), and in Visual mode. A mark moves with its text, and goes when its line is deleted (undo brings it back). :marks lists them. They live in memory, one set for each file; A-Z and 0-9 are not marks here.

column3: go to the line of a mark
column4: Goes to the first non-blank of the line of the mark you type: a motion by lines, so d'a deletes the lines from here to there. With a mark that is not set it says mark not set and does nothing.

column3: go to the place of a mark
column4: Goes to the line and the column of the mark you type: a motion by characters, so d`a deletes up to it, not including it.

column3: back to before the last jump
column4: Goes to the line of the place the cursor was at before the last jump (G, gg, /, n, N, *, #, %, a mark, :s, u), and the place left becomes the one to go back to: '' twice is a round trip. A jump that goes nowhere leaves it as it was.

column3: back to before the last jump (place)
column4: Like '', to the place and not the line.

Opens the command line: :w saves, :q quits, :s/old/new/ substitutes, :{n} goes to line n, :{range}!cmd filters, :help shows this table. In Visual mode it starts with the selection as the range, '<,'>.
Searches forward as you type (the screen follows the first match; Esc goes back), then Enter keeps the place and lights the matches. Smartcase: a capital makes the search exact. n and N go on.
Like /, looking back.

Saves the file in every mode (Insert mode stays Insert mode), as :w does. It is refused, and says so, when the disk changed since the file was read and the changes conflict with yours: :w! keeps yours, :e! takes the disk's, and each copies the version it gives up.
Saves if there are changes and closes the file, as :x does.
Closes the file and discards the changes, as :q! does.
Closes the file as :q does (less's q: sim has no macros). With changes it says no write since last change. The last file open ends sim.
Scrolls so that the cursor's line is in the middle of the screen.
Moves to the next change that came from the disk (another process, a build, an agent) and has not been looked at; the mark goes when the cursor reaches it. :seen clears all the marks.
Moves to the previous change that came from the disk and has not been looked at.
Shows the next open file, wrapping round. The status line (and the tabs) say which one of how many: 2/3. With the tree focused it works too.
Shows the previous open file, wrapping round.
Opens the tree of the project and focuses it, or closes it when it already has the focus. In the picker it moves down the list.
Opens the finder: type to find a file by any characters of its path, in order; Enter opens it. In the picker it moves up the list.
Opens the search of the contents of the files (ripgrep if it is on the PATH): results grouped by file with a preview, the match bold; Enter opens the file at the match. Not in plain mode.

Opens this table of keys and commands as a picker, filtered as you type; the longer text of the entry under the cursor is in the preview. Enter and Esc close it, and it runs nothing. :help does the same.
Turns the syntax colors of the text on or off, for every file; the message says which.
Goes round the looks (calm, flat, depth); the choice is remembered. In plain mode the look stays calm.
Turns the icons of the tree, the tabs and the status line on or off; the choice is remembered. They need a Nerd Font, which a terminal does not announce.
Space starts a sequence, as the leader of the author's Neovim does: <Space>bp and <Space>bc. Space followed by a key that has no sequence does nothing; where Space is text it is the character.
The files that are open, as tabs: pick one by its letter, or pick one to close; <Space>bk says where the version a save or a reload gave up went.

Puts a letter on each tab (bufferline's: the first letter of the file's name when it is free, else the next one of its alphabet), and the letter you type shows that file. Esc or any other key cancels. Without a tab bar the letters are on the status line.

Puts a letter on each tab as <Space>bp does, and the letter you type closes that file as :q would: a file with changes is not closed, it says so and its tab is shown. sim never closes a file with unsaved work.

Says again, alone on the status line, where the version that :w! or :e! gave up was copied (SAFE-7): a path a shell takes, ~/... below the home directory. A path wider than the line is cut from the left, so that the file's name stays. Before any copy it says so.
What git has to say: <Space>ge shows what differs from HEAD, <Space>gi what the guard did to this repository. In sim --plain, which runs no program, there is none.

Opens the panel in the changes view: only the files that differ from HEAD (staged and unstaged together, untracked ones too) in their folders, each with its letter (M changed, A added, D deleted, R renamed, U untracked) and +n −n from git diff --numstat HEAD, a folder with the sums. Enter on a deleted file opens HEAD's version, read-only; a rename is one row, old → new. <Space>ge again, or q, goes back to the tree. In sim --plain it is refused: plain mode runs no program.

Says again, on the status line, what sim did about this repository's config (GIT-5): why git was not run, with the key and the file; or the settings of the repository's own that it turned off (the monitor, the hooks path, a filter, an external diff), by name; or that there is none. The tree's box says the short form for as long as it is true. In sim --plain, which runs no program, it says so.
Toggles of the interface: <Space>um turns the read view of Markdown on and off.

Turns the read view of Markdown files on or off, for every file; the message says which. On, every line but the cursor's and the selected ones is drawn as it reads: the markers of emphasis and of inline code are not drawn, and a table is aligned by the width of its cells; the line you are on is always the file's own text. Off, the file is drawn as it is. The choice is remembered. In sim --plain there is no read view.
Moves the cursor one row down the tree.
Moves the cursor one row up the tree.
Opens the directory under the cursor, or opens the file and gives it the focus; on an open directory it does nothing.
Closes the directory under the cursor, or moves to its parent.
Moves to the first row.
Moves to the last row.
Moves the cursor half the panel down.
Moves the cursor half the panel up.
Moves the cursor a panel down.
Moves the cursor a panel up.

Types a query: the paths that match, and the folders leading to them, light up in place and nothing moves; Enter opens the best match, Esc puts everything back. n and N go from match to match afterwards.
After a find in the tree, goes to the next or the previous match.
Narrows the tree to the files that changed, are open, or were opened recently; again to widen it.
Closes every directory; the cursor stays on the top-level entry that held it.
Closes the panel; the text has the focus. In the changes view (<Space>ge) it goes back to the tree instead.
Gives the focus back to the text and leaves the panel open.
Moves the selection down the list; the preview follows.
Moves the selection up the list; the preview follows.
Moves the selection a list's height.
Opens the selected file at its match and closes the picker; in the help it only closes it.
Closes the picker; everything is as it was.
Clears the query.
Deletes the last word of the query.
Deletes the last character of the query; at an empty query it closes the picker.
Inserts a tab, or the file's own indent.
Deletes the character before the cursor, or joins the line to the one above.
Breaks the line, keeping the indent.
The arrow keys, Home and End move the cursor without leaving Insert mode.

:w saves; :w {file} saves under another name (not over a file that exists); :w! writes anyway: over a file without write permission, and over a version on the disk that conflicts with yours after copying that version into the state directory.
Saves, and closes the file when the save is done. :x saves only if there are changes.
:q closes the file; with changes it says no write since last change (:q! to override). :q! discards them. The last file open ends sim.
Quits with exit code 1, which makes git abort a commit whose message is being edited.

:e {file} opens another file in a tab, or shows it if it is open; :e! reloads this one from the disk, copying yours into the state directory first when they conflict. In plain mode :e replaces the file.
:qa quits when no file has changes; :qa! discards them all; :wa saves every modified file and leaves out the ones that conflict with the disk, naming them. Not in plain mode.
:s/old/new/ replaces the first match in the line, with g every match; :%s/old/new/g does the whole file. A pattern is a regex; & in the replacement is what matched, \1 a group.
:42 moves to line 42; :$ to the last line; :'<,'> is the Visual selection.
Runs the lines of the range through sh -c cmd and replaces them with its output, as one undo step; typing goes on meanwhile and Ctrl-c cancels. :%!sort sorts the file. Not in plain mode.
Forgets the marks of the changes that came from the disk, as if they had all been looked at.
Puts the lit matches of the search out and the count with them; n or a new search lights them again.

:registers shows what each register holds, the unnamed one first, a line break as ⏎, long text cut to fit the line; a register that holds nothing is left out. Nothing is written to the disk: they are gone when sim ends.

:marks shows each mark that is set, a to z and ' (the place before the last jump), with its line and column and the text of its line, on one line cut to fit it. Nothing is written to the disk: they are gone when the file is closed.
:help (or :h, or F1) opens this table; :help words opens it with the words typed.
